courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: How a stale CAS corrupts a lock-free stack
md: CAS checks *equality of value*, not *absence of change*. Any algorithm that reads a pointer, computes from what it points to, and then CASes on that pointer is wrong if the pointed-to node can be recycled in between.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
md: Add-one-in measures a stage in isolation; leave-one-out measures its marginal value in the system you will ship. When the two disagree, the stages interact, and that disagreement is itself a finding worth reporting.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Case: First American Financial and 885 million documents (2019)
md: First American had two failures. The code failure was a missing object-level check. The process failure was treating a confirmed exposure of hundreds of millions of sensitive documents as low severity. Severity comes from what the bug exposes, not from how simple the bug is.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Testing authorization with role matrices, and detecting enumeration
md: Authorization is tested by asking the wrong user. For every endpoint, decide in advance what anonymous users, other users, other tenants and admins should get, write it down as a matrix, and make the build fail when reality differs.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberoasting: service tickets that can be cracked offline
md: Kerberoasting works because any user may request any service ticket and the ticket is locked with a key derived from the service account's password. Remove human passwords from service accounts (gMSA), drop RC4, keep them unprivileged, and alert on RC4 4769s for user-owned SPNs.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: When the DC itself has the bug: Zerologon, noPac, PrintNightmare
md: DC bugs turn a foothold into the domain in minutes, so DCs are patched first and fastest, run no extra services, and go to enforcement mode early. Zerologon, noPac and PrintNightmare each have specific events to watch.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Case: Follina (CVE-2022-30190), a document with no macro
md: Patches end a bug; detections outlive it. Word starting msdt.exe was abnormal before May 2022 and is still abnormal now, so the behaviour rule keeps catching the next abuse of a protocol handler.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Ransomware crypto mistakes: how Hive's files were decrypted
md: Never use one keystream twice. Reusing keystream material across files turns any file whose original you hold into a key for others. Sound designs encrypt each file with its own key from a proper cipher and protect the master secret with public-key encryption.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Exploit chains: renderer bug, sandbox escape, kernel bug
md: A full compromise of a hardened platform is a chain, usually renderer RCE plus sandbox escape plus kernel bug. Each extra wall forces another 0-day, and each stage is a separate chance to detect or break the attack.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Running a purple team exercise
md: A purple team exercise is a loop per technique: context, expectation, execution, investigation, fix, retest, record. The output is not a list of what the red team achieved but a list of what the blue team can now see that it could not see in the morning.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: SWE-bench: how one patch gets graded
md: Resolved means: the patch applies, and **every** FAIL_TO_PASS test and **every** PASS_TO_PASS test is found and passes. Fixing the issue while breaking one old test scores exactly the same as doing nothing.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Designing tools: the agent-computer interface
md: Treat tool design like UI design for a new colleague: clear names, documented parameters, concise high-signal output, guardrails that turn likely mistakes into instructive errors. Changing the tool often beats changing the prompt.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why an agent saying done is not evidence of done
md: Verification turns "the agent says it is done" into "independent evidence says it is done". How much you can trust a shipped result is bounded by how often the verifier passes wrong results.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Sandboxes at scale: throughput, stragglers and reward hacking
md: Treat the environment as part of the training algorithm. Its reward defines what is learned, its isolation defines what can be cheated, and its throughput (containers times 3600 divided by episode seconds) defines how many steps you can afford.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: The lethal trifecta and excessive agency
md: "Read-only" tools are not harmless in a trifecta. A tool that only fetches URLs is a perfect exit: the data goes out in the request.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: MCP and agent tools: when tool descriptions are the attack
md: Every MCP server you add is code you run and text your model obeys. Install few, from publishers you trust; pin and review their descriptions; show full arguments on approval; sandbox local servers; and do not combine private-data tools, untrusted-content tools and outbound tools in one agent.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
md: Materials generators are diffusion models over a mixed object (types, periodic coordinates, lattice). They change where candidates come from; MLIPs and DFT still decide which are stable, and novelty must be checked against experimental databases.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Second-generation text watermarks: unbiased, semantic, code, multi-bit
md: Each second-generation scheme buys one property with another: exact distributions with model-dependent tests or zero robustness gains, paraphrase robustness with slow rejection sampling, code detection with model access, user ids with more text, public verification with long outputs. Pick the property your use case cannot live without.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
md: Masking is the main failure of mean-based scores: several outliers inflate the standard deviation and hide one another. The NIST handbook also warns that applying a single-outlier test repeatedly does not fix this, because the first test may already report nothing.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Evaluating detectors when 1 percent of points are anomalies
md: Do not report accuracy for anomaly detection: labeling everything normal scores 99 percent accuracy here. Be wary of ROC-AUC alone too. Report AP or a PR curve, plus precision@k at the review budget you actually have.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OAuth 2.0: delegated access without sharing a password
md: Misconception: "Sign in with X" means OAuth logged you in. Plain OAuth only says some client got a token. Building login on raw access tokens has caused real impersonation bugs; OpenID Connect adds the missing pieces.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Validating a JWT correctly: algorithm, signature, iss, aud, exp, nbf
md: Validation is a fixed checklist the receiver owns: pinned algorithm, trusted issuer's key, signature, iss, aud, exp and nbf with small leeway, type. A library helps only when you pass it every one of those rules.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Three maps of a secure SDLC: Microsoft SDL, OWASP SAMM, NIST SSDF
md: SDL says what one company does, SAMM measures how mature you are, and SSDF is the reference list that governments and customers ask you to attest to. Most programmes use SAMM to plan and SSDF to report. You will also meet BSIMM (Building Security In Maturity Model), which describes what real companies' programmes do rather than prescribing a target.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Secrets scanning and pre-commit hooks
md: Rewriting git history to remove a secret does not un-leak it. Forks, clones, CI caches and anyone who fetched in the meantime still have it. Treat any committed secret as compromised: rotate it, then look at the provider's logs for its use.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Programme decisions: secure defaults, memory safety, Secure by Design
md: Finding bugs is linear work; removing bug classes compounds. A mature programme spends part of its budget on defaults, paved roads and language choices that make the next thousand findings never happen.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Why a question is not a short version of its answer
md: Search is asymmetric. Queries and documents differ in length, form and role, and relevance means *answers*, not *looks like*. Tell the model which side each text is on.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Retries that do not stampede: backoff, jitter and Retry-After
md: Retry with: honor Retry-After when present (plus a little randomness); otherwise capped exponential backoff with full jitter; a maximum number of attempts and a total time budget; and retries only for retryable errors (429, 5xx, timeouts), never for 400-class mistakes (4xx codes such as 400 Bad Request mean the request itself is wrong, so it fails the same way again), billing or quota errors.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
md: The bug is the gap between the read and the write. Any fix must make the whole read-modify-write indivisible, either with a lock around it or with an atomic operation.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score
md: Do not apply softmax across AudioSet classes and then threshold. A clip with dog and speech would have to split probability between them. Use the model's per-class sigmoid scores, and tune a threshold per class if you need hard yes/no tags.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Password rules that work: NIST SP 800-63B
md: Forced periodic rotation makes passwords weaker, not stronger: people make the smallest possible change. CISA's advisory on Scattered Spider (a cybercriminal group that targets companies through their IT help desks, lesson 12) repeats NIST's advice to refrain from recurring password changes. Change on evidence of compromise instead.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: SSO at a glance, detection signals, and responding to takeover
md: Identity attacks leave traces in authentication logs: failures, travel, new devices, MFA changes. Centralising login through SSO makes those traces easy to collect, and makes the IdP the account to protect most.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: One API in front of many models: the Converse call
md: `inferenceConfig` has only four fields. Putting a model-specific parameter there is a mistake; it belongs in `additionalModelRequestFields`, and it only works for models that define it.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Reading decompiler output critically
md: A decompiler's output is a hypothesis built from guesses about functions, conventions and types. Each fix you make (define a function, set a signature, apply a struct) removes a guess, and the output improves everywhere that information flows.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers
md: bitnet.cpp's kernels are **lossless**: they reproduce the training-time quantization exactly. On 1,000 prompts with a 700M BitNet b1.58 model, I2_S, TL1 and TL2 matched an FP32 reference token for token 100% of the time, versus 1.4% for llama.cpp's own ternary formats TQ1_0 and TQ2_0, which quantize activations in 256-element blocks unlike training.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: When branchless loses, and how to measure it
md: Agner Fog's rule of thumb: a conditional jump beats a conditional move when the code is part of a dependency chain and prediction is better than about 75 percent. For random binary-search keys (about 50 percent) cmov wins; for keys that cluster, the branch wins.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes
md: No engine minimizes read, write and space amplification at once. B+trees pay on random writes. Leveled LSMs pay in rewrites. Tiered LSMs pay in reads and temporary space. Pick the cost your workload can afford, then tune T, Bloom bits and compaction bandwidth.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Business impact analysis: from processes to tolerable downtime
md: Do not let IT set the MTD by asking "how fast could we restore it?". That gives you the current capability, not the requirement. The BIA asks the process owner "how long until this becomes unacceptable?", and the gap between the two answers is the work of the rest of this course.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Restoring at the right size: Atlassian's two-week outage, April 2022
md: Granularity is a recovery requirement. In multi-tenant systems (one data store, many customers), "restore the database" also rolls back every unaffected customer. Write RTOs per restore size (one record, one tenant, many tenants, everything) and test each, because they are different procedures with very different times.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Crisis management: decisions, workarounds and communication
md: Do not let the recovery team be the crisis team. Engineers in the middle of a restore should not also be negotiating with customers and drafting press statements; and executives should not be choosing which database snapshot to restore. Separate the roles, connect them with a fixed reporting rhythm.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Build it: a byte GPT, then a two-level patch model
md: A byte GPT is a GPT with a 256-entry vocabulary; the cost is more positions per byte. A two-level model fixes that by running the big network once per patch, and stays causal only through two shifts: one patch for the global input, one byte for the local input.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Why C memory bugs compile cleanly and ship
md: Tools such as AddressSanitizer and **fuzzing** (feeding the program huge numbers of automatically generated or mutated inputs and watching for crashes) find many of these bugs, but only on inputs that actually run. The Android team describes them as treating symptoms rather than the root cause, and notes that coverage stays low without constant pressure on teams to fuzz and triage.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Build a safe type on unsafe: a minimal Vec from scratch
md: Recipe for an unsafe-backed type: write the invariants down, keep the fields they mention private, make every unsafe block's SAFETY comment cite one invariant, and run tests that hit the edges (empty, first grow, full, drop with live elements) under Miri.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Where a line may live: sets, ways and tags
md: Capacity is set by size, conflicts by associativity and address bits. A bigger cache fixes capacity misses; more ways or a less regular stride fixes conflict misses; nothing but prefetching (loading lines before the program asks for them, lesson 4) hides cold misses.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Pruning by influence and grouping supernodes
md: Influence is unsigned. A feature that strongly *inhibits* the answer scores as high as one that promotes it. Use influence to decide what to look at, then read the signed edges to decide what it does.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Inverse propensity scoring turns clicks into unbiased labels
md: Only clicked documents need propensities, and the estimate is unbiased only if the propensities are correct and every relevant document has a nonzero chance of being observed. Joachims et al. also require that propensities depend only on logged information (unconfoundedness).

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Framework auto-escaping and its escape hatches
md: "It comes from our own API" is not the same as "trusted". The value was typed by some user before your API stored it. React's own Markdown example is safe only because the rendered HTML is shown back to the same user who wrote it, and because the team trusts the Markdown parser to have no bugs.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Temperature: why CLIP multiplies cosines by up to 100
md: The temperature turns a ranking of small cosine gaps into a confident probability. Its value decides how sharply the loss concentrates on hard negatives, which is why CLIP learns it and caps the logit scale at 100 for stability.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Your own rules: key abuse, persistence and log tampering
md: Misconception: "ATT&CK IDs are permanent". MITRE reorganises the matrix: Disable or Modify Cloud Log moved from T1562.008 to T1685.002, and tactics have been renamed. Map rules to IDs, but review the mapping when a new ATT&CK version ships.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Code Spaces 2014: why one account is one blast radius
md: Design as if any one credential will be stolen tomorrow. The test of an architecture is not "can an attacker get in?" but "what can one stolen login destroy or read?" Keep the data and its last good copy behind different identities, in different accounts.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Azure in depth: role assignments, Run Command and PIM
md: In Azure, the keys to escalation are writing role assignments and running code where a privileged identity lives. Make powerful roles eligible through PIM, delegate assignments with conditions instead of Owner, and treat Virtual Machine Contributor on a VM as equal to that VM's managed identity.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Long-lived keys vs temporary credentials: STS and Uber 2016
md: Prefer roles and temporary credentials everywhere. AWS's own best practices say to require human users to use federation with temporary credentials and to require workloads to use IAM roles. Long-term access keys are for the few cases nothing else supports, and they need rotation, monitoring and the narrowest possible permissions.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: What k-means actually optimises
md: Scaling is a modelling choice, not a cleanup step. Standardising says "one standard deviation of every feature counts the same", which silently gives a noisy, unimportant feature as much say as a crucial one. Decide how much each feature should weigh, then scale to match. k-means, DBSCAN's eps and every method in this course measure distance, and none of them is scale free.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Evaluating a clustering with and without labels
md: Look at the first two bars. The k = 2 clustering with the *better* inertia, 28.8333, scores ARI 0.4109, while the local optimum with the worse inertia, 30.4167, scores 0.7734. Optimising the objective harder moved the answer away from the truth. Inertia is a proxy, and this is what it means for a proxy to be imperfect: never argue from inertia to correctness.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: SIMD, compiled queries and where columnar engines hit limits
md: Columnar storage cuts bytes moved; vectorized execution cuts instructions per byte. SIMD multiplies the second only when data is dense and in cache.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Why code breaks at -O2: undefined behavior as an optimization license
md: The optimizer assumes the program has no UB: signed overflow never happens, differently typed pointers never alias, dereferenced pointers are not null. Code that breaks those rules can change behavior at -O2. Find it with sanitizers and the -fwrapv, -fno-strict-aliasing and -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks switches, then fix the code.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
md: A computer-use agent is an ordinary agent loop where the tool is "the computer" and the observation is a screenshot. The model proposes actions in screenshot pixel coordinates; the harness executes them, and is the only place you can enforce scaling, safety and verification.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
md: loom only sees what goes through loom types. A `std::sync::Mutex` or a third-party lock inside your code still runs, but loom cannot schedule around it, so executions that are possible in reality are silently not modeled. Libraries you depend on need loom support too for full coverage.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
md: Consistency models learn the end of the ODE trajectory, not its slope. The boundary condition anchors the chain at the data; adjacent-time agreement (from a teacher's ODE step or from the data itself) propagates it to high noise; extra steps re-noise and jump again to trade compute for quality.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: The hash ring: each key goes to the next node clockwise
md: Consistent hashing minimises *movement*. It does not by itself give *balance*. With one random token per node, arcs vary wildly in size, as the toy ring shows. The next lesson fixes that.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Why scheduling explodes, and what a constraint model is
md: A constraint solver separates **what** a solution is (the model) from **how** to find it (the search). You declare variables, domains and constraints; the solver chooses the order of guesses and the deductions. Adding a rule means adding one constraint, not rewriting a search loop.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
md: A container is a fenced process on a shared kernel. Threat-model it as "attacker has a shell in this process" and ask which credentials, network paths and kernel interfaces that shell can touch.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: The API server is the front door: authn, authz, admission
md: Every request passes authentication (401 if unknown), authorization (403 if not allowed), then admission (mutate, then validate) before etcd. Reads skip admission, so RBAC alone protects them. Turn on audit logging, because it is off unless you configure it.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Network policies: from default allow to default deny
md: Pods are non-isolated until a policy selects them. Start each namespace with default deny for both directions, add DNS, then add one allow per intended connection, on both sides.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
md: No single control holds. Minimal signed images, Restricted pods, least-privilege RBAC, default-deny networks, encrypted and narrowly readable Secrets, authenticated node APIs, patched runtimes, and two kinds of detection: each covers what the others miss.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: Do not ask the LLM to copy job ids out of text. Give it the shown list with positions and attributes and let it output a position or an attribute match; code does the lookup. A model that types ids can produce a well-formed id that was never shown.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Hidden computation: filler tokens, encoded reasoning, paraphrasing
md: Misconception: "filler tokens did not help, so all of a model's reasoning must be in the words." Lanham's result shows that particular models did not learn to use filler. Pfau et al. show training can teach a transformer to compute across meaningless tokens on suitable problems, and nothing in a monitor's view of "......" would reveal what was computed.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
md: These methods sit uneasily with "keep optimization pressure off the CoT". VFT trains directly on CoT content. The difference from Baker et al.'s failure is direction and timing: it rewards saying more, before RL, and the RL reward never reads the CoT. VFT was tested on one 8B model with multiple-choice cues; whether it holds for frontier agents is open.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
md: A larger max_length is not free and not always possible. Position embeddings fix the hard limit at training time (512 for BERT), and compute per pair grows with sequence length. For long documents, chunk and take the max (or another aggregate) instead of hoping truncation keeps the right part.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Encoding, hashing and encryption are three different things
md: A hash of a short or guessable value is not secret. There are only 10,000 four-digit PINs; hashing all of them takes a fraction of a second, so a stored SHA-256 of a PIN is as good as the PIN. Lesson 11 covers how passwords must be stored instead.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: RSA with tiny numbers: encryption, signing and padding
md: If you ever write pow(m, e, n) in production code you have built textbook RSA. Call a library's OAEP or PSS function, or better, avoid RSA encryption entirely and use an elliptic-curve key exchange plus an AEAD.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Signature nonces: reuse, weak randomness and deterministic signing
md: Two identical signatures of the same message are harmless with RFC 6979. The alarm is the same r value on two different messages under one key: that means k repeated, and the private key must be considered public.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
md: Intensity per tile is not the whole story. Two CTAs that share a row of tiles both read the same slice of A, and the L2 cache may serve the second read. CUTLASS's threadblock rasterization (swizzling the CTA launch order: remapping launch indices to tile coordinates so that CTAs running at the same time cover a compact patch of tiles rather than one long row) exists to make that L2 reuse more likely.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs
md: A tile that maximizes arithmetic intensity can still lose: it may leave a tail wave, spill registers, or leave too little shared memory for stages. Measure with the CUTLASS profiler across candidate configurations rather than trusting one formula.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
md: "It was public, so it was allowed" is the most common mistake. The ACM Code of Ethics says it directly: "A system being publicly accessible is not sufficient grounds on its own to imply authorization." Lesson 4 shows the opposite mistake too: officials calling ordinary viewing of a public page a crime.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
md: CMA: s1 knowingly unauthorised access attempt (2 years); s2 with intent to commit a further offence (5); s3 unauthorised impairment (10); s3ZA serious damage (14 or life); s3A tools for those offences (2). Authorisation must come from someone entitled to control that kind of access.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
md: Wassenaar (2013, amended 2017) controls intrusion software platforms and development technology, with carve-outs for vulnerability disclosure and incident response. The US implements it through BIS's 2021 rule and License Exception ACE; destination, end user and intended unauthorised use decide when a licence is needed.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
md: When the problem is your own organisation: record the facts, escalate internally to the top, take legal advice, and use lawful external channels (regulators, law enforcement) if ignored. Never relabel a breach, pay for silence, or mislead an investigator.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Fitting a mixing law: RegMix, data mixing laws, judging a mixture
md: Regression methods learn mixture to loss from many cheap runs and search the fit. They work when the fitted function has the right shape and accurate parameters: a linear fit picks a corner, and mis-set laws can lose to uniform weights. Always compare against stratified sampling, and judge data choices with small models scored on continuous metrics.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Counting cache lines: the traffic model and the padding bonus
md: Traffic ratio for a streaming loop is $S/k$: record size over bytes touched. For random access to whole records, the ratio flips against SoA by up to the number of fields.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Keep less: minimisation, retention schedules and legal holds
md: Deleting the primary copy is not deletion. Exports, tickets, caches, logs and backups each need their own retention, and backups usually expire last. Lesson 13 shows a way to make old backups unreadable all at once: encrypt them and destroy the key.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Where DLP acts: endpoints, email, web and cloud
md: Every exception is a hole. Allowlisting a whole team, a whole domain or a whole application because one rule was noisy removes protection from every future leak through that path. Fix the detector, then make narrow, reviewed exceptions with an expiry date.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Why distributed bugs refuse to reproduce
md: DST makes a run a pure function of (code, seed). Faults can then be as aggressive and random as you like, because any failure they provoke can be replayed exactly by re-running one seed.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: CircleCI 2023: when the platform holding your secrets is breached
md: Encryption at rest did not save the secrets, because a running service must decrypt them to use them, and the attacker read the keys from a running process. The only secret a breached CI vendor cannot leak is one it never stored.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest
md: A sampling step is: one forward pass over the whole sequence, a guess at every masked slot, then keep the k most confident guesses and remask the rest. The schedule fixes k per step; the confidence ranking decides the order.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
md: Prefill is compute-bound and sets TTFT; decode is memory-bound and sets TPOT. Putting both in one batch makes each phase pay for the other.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: From sectors to partitions to image files
md: Do not stop at the partitions. NIST SP 800-86 counts *free space* (areas not allocated to any partition, including whole deleted volumes) as a place where data may remain. Our lab disk already has 2,047 sectors before the first partition that no file system owns.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics from the defender's side: what each trick leaves
md: The cleanup is evidence too. A 1102 event, a reset journal or deleted shadow copies at 14:35 tell you someone with administrator rights was covering tracks then, which often dates the intrusion better than anything they deleted.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
md: DPO is not "RLHF without a reward". It fits the same Bradley-Terry reward model, just parameterized through the policy. It also inherits the KL objective's $\beta$. What it removes is the separate reward network and on-policy sampling during training.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
md: Until phase 4, at least one store is complete and current, and the other one is being kept in step with it. That is what makes every earlier step reversible. Plan each phase so it can be rolled out gradually (by percentage of objects or code paths) and rolled back with a flag.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
md: Move one thing at a time, keep one store complete until the very end, and measure agreement continuously. The deletion in phase 4 is the only step that should be hard to undo.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Affine quantization: storing reals as int8 plus a scale
md: Misconception: int8 means the model can only represent values between -128 and 127. The integers are codes; the scale maps them to any real range. What int8 limits is the number of distinct levels (256) inside that range, so the range you pick matters more than the bit width alone.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Ivanti Connect Secure, 2024: chained zero-days and a fooled checker
md: A clean integrity check is evidence, not proof. If an attacker reached root, the checker ran on a system the attacker controls. Trust measurements taken from outside the device, and rebuild when root was possible.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Overthinking: 901 tokens to say 2 + 3 = 5
md: Efficient reasoning asks a different question from test-time scaling. Not 'does more thinking help?' but 'how few thinking tokens reach the same accuracy on this particular problem?'

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Underthinking and early exit: stopping at the right moment
md: Long output does not tell you which failure you have. Overthinking re-solves an easy problem that was already right; underthinking abandons a promising approach on a hard one. The fixes differ: stop earlier in the first case, stay longer on each idea in the second.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: ETW: providers, sessions and consumers
md: ETW is plumbing: providers emit, sessions buffer, consumers read. Most of what Event Viewer, Sysmon and EDR sensors show you rides on it, so an attacker who can switch providers off removes evidence before it is ever written.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Tampering and EDR killers: SUNBURST, BYOVD and AuKill
md: Check your driver-load filter against this case. SwiftOnSecurity's config excludes event 6 for drivers whose signature contains `microsoft`. The driver AuKill abused was signed by Microsoft, so that exclusion would hide its load. Narrow exclusions to drivers you have inventoried, or match against a vulnerable-driver hash list instead of the signer.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Neural NILM, seq2point, and the unseen-house problem
md: Every NILM method injects prior knowledge to resolve an unidentifiable sum. Hart hand-designs it (step signatures), FHMMs encode it as state machines, and neural nets learn it from sub-metered houses. The test that matters is a house the model never saw.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings
md: General-purpose embedding models do not know your abbreviations (`SWE` software engineer, `SDET` software development engineer in test, `RN` registered nurse) and blur words that share context (`sales engineer` vs `software engineer`). Expand abbreviations before embedding, match against many alternate titles rather than one label, and keep an *unknown* outcome instead of forcing the nearest code.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Delegated vs application permissions, and who may consent
md: Delegated means the app is capped by the user; application means the app is capped only by the permission. Restrict who may consent to what, and treat every application permission, especially any with write access, as an admin role held by software.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Devices and the Primary Refresh Token: SSO bound to hardware
md: The PRT is the device's master refresh token. Its strength is the TPM-held session key that signs every use; its weak points are devices without TPMs, attacker-registered devices, and the fact that Conditional Access runs when it is used, not when it is issued.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Taking over admins: help desks, MFA resets and rogue federation
md: Help-desk takeovers turn a phone call into admin credentials, and admin credentials into persistence (federated domains, app secrets, devices). Verify callers out of band, keep admin resets in a small privileged role, require phishing-resistant MFA for admins, and alert on any federation change.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Level-triggered asks "is it ready now?" on every wait. Edge-triggered says "it just became ready" once. With ET you own the state: read or write until `EAGAIN`, or remember that the connection is still ready.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Testing many variants: Bonferroni and Holm corrections
md: Count every comparison you make on a query set, including metrics, variants and earlier papers' tests, and correct for the family. Holm is never worse than Bonferroni. Better still, decide the one comparison you will test before you look.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: RELRO, the GOT and FORTIFY_SOURCE
md: RELRO protects a table of pointers by making it read-only after start-up; FORTIFY stops some overflows before they write. Both are cheap, both are build flags, and both should be on: `-Wl,-z,relro,-z,now` and `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3` at `-O2`.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: How big is a line, how to find false sharing, who pads
md: Do not pad on a hunch. Padding costs memory and can push other hot data out of cache, which is why Drepper calls padding every variable unacceptable. Confirm with perf c2c or a before-and-after benchmark that the line is really contended.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Why a filter breaks greedy search on an HNSW graph
md: Predicate subgraph traversal is the right search strategy (no distance computations wasted on failing nodes), but on a normal HNSW graph the predicate subgraph is sparse and disconnected. ACORN changes how the graph is built, or how neighbors are looked up, so that the predicate subgraph stays connected for any predicate.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Build it: a DeepSeekMoE layer with bias balancing in your GPT
md: Do not read quality conclusions off a run this small. Character-level Shakespeare with a 3.65M-parameter MoE (0.9M active) trains in under an hour per run on a CPU; differences of a few thousandths in validation loss between configurations are within seed noise. What this lab shows reliably is the mechanism: what the router does without balancing, and how each method changes the expert loads.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
md: FlashInfer = one block-sparse view of every KV layout, attention states merged exactly so work can be split and composed freely, a per-step plan that balances skewed lengths while staying CUDA-graph friendly, and a JIT template so new variants get fused kernels instead of new libraries.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Inductive invariants: from bounded checks to every N
md: An invariant is true in reachable states; an inductive invariant is preserved from *any* state that satisfies it. Model checking finds the first; proofs need the second. Use TLC or Apalache to debug a candidate before you try to prove it. Verus loop invariants, later in the course, carry the same three obligations.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Connecting specs to running code, and the wider tool map
md: Trace validation is testing, not proof: it checks only the runs you logged, and its verdict depends on choosing the right points in the code to log each atomic step. The paper says plainly that it does not provide formal correctness guarantees. Its strength is that it keeps a spec honest at the cost of logging.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Microscaling: one power-of-two scale per 32 values
md: MX formats move fine-grained scaling into hardware: 32 elements share one power-of-two E8M0 scale, applied by the tensor core during the dot product. For 8-bit elements that works well. For 4-bit elements the power-of-two restriction can waste up to a whole binade of FP4's tiny 3.58-binade range.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Scraping and enumeration: Facebook's 530 million phone numbers
md: Any feature that answers "is this identifier on the service, and whose is it" is an enumeration oracle. Cap it, gate it on consent, minimise its answer and watch its traffic.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fake accounts and Sybil attacks
md: You cannot prove two accounts are two people (Douceur). Make each identity cost something scarce, give new accounts limited power until they earn trust, and look for accounts that act as a group.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Chargebacks, disputes and the true cost of a fraudulent order
md: Chargebacks are the fraud label, and they arrive weeks to months late. A fraudulent order costs goods, shipping and fees, several good orders' worth of margin.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Privacy and fairness of risk models
md: Collect what measurably helps, keep it only as long as needed, and keep it out of other uses. Then measure who your false positives are: an acceptable average can hide an unacceptable burden on one group.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: What vulnerability research is, and the rules you work under
md: Vulnerability research is a loop of find, triage, root-cause, report, fix. Its output is a fixed bug and a regression test, not an exploit, and it starts with permission.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Continuous fuzzing at scale: OSS-Fuzz, ClusterFuzz and Heartbleed
md: Continuous fuzzing turns fuzzing from an event into a property of the project: every commit is fuzzed, every crash is triaged, and fixed reproducers keep guarding the code. If your project parses untrusted input, it belongs in OSS-Fuzz or in ClusterFuzzLite (a lightweight version of ClusterFuzz that runs fuzzers in your CI pipeline).

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing the report and coordinating disclosure
md: Report privately with a minimised reproducer, the sanitizer output, a one-sentence root cause and a suggested fix; agree a disclosure date; publish an advisory with versions and credit once users can patch.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
md: A hard bin boundary is fragile: noise of a few thousandths can push u from 0.249 to 0.251 and the vote goes to the wrong bin. Practical systems search neighboring bins, or, like Astrometry.net, skip fixed bins and do a radius search in continuous code space.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Distance on a sphere, and why degree boxes break
md: Use great-circle distance for the final answer. The sphere itself is a model: the Earth is slightly flattened, and a spherical model gives errors typically up to 0.3%. That is why PostGIS `geography` defaults to `use_spheroid = true`, and Elasticsearch `geo_distance` defaults to `distance_type: arc` (the faster `plane` is documented as inaccurate over long distances and near the poles).

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Batching: why 32 launches lose to one
md: The per-image resize kernel does 0.44 microseconds of memory work and carries 0.9 to 6.7 microseconds of launch overhead. The GPU is idle or draining for most of the wall clock, and no kernel tuning can recover it. The fix is one launch that covers the whole batch.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Expandable segments: growing one segment with virtual memory
md: Fixed segments freeze their size at cudaMalloc time, so shapes that drift leave slivers. Expandable segments separate virtual addresses from physical memory (reserve once, map chunks as needed), so the segment grows contiguously instead.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
md: Bank = word index mod 32. Different words in one bank serialize; the same word broadcasts. For column access to a 2D tile, make the row width odd.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
md: SOL percentages are not the score you optimize. The triage guide is blunt about it: validate every change against absolute kernel duration, because SOL percentages can drop while the kernel gets faster, for example when you reduce the total work. Duration is the ground truth, not SOL percent.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
md: GraphRAG moves work from query time to indexing time. It pays many LLM calls up front to turn the corpus into a graph and a set of pre-written community summaries, so that global questions can be answered by reading summaries instead of sampling chunks.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
md: Failure modes to watch in any LLM-built graph: missed entities in large chunks, duplicate nodes from name variants, hallucinated relationships stated with confidence, and summaries that drop the specific quotes users need. Every later stage inherits these errors, and global answers rarely show the raw evidence.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
md: "The model discovered reasoning on its own" is an overstatement. Liu et al. (2025, the Dr. GRPO paper you will meet in lesson 7) found that DeepSeek-V3-Base already shows aha-moment style self-reflection before any RL, and the R1 authors themselves say the vivid first-person reasoning style reflects engineered heuristics in the cold-start data. RL amplified behaviors already present in the base model.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
md: Time profiles answer *where*. Counters answer *why*: low IPC plus many cache misses points at memory, many branch misses points at prediction, high IPC with lots of instructions points at doing too much work.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Power, EM, sound and faults: physical side channels
md: Physical side channels need the attacker close to the device, but that is exactly the threat model of smart cards, phones, payment terminals, hardware wallets and secure enclaves. Hertzbleed shows the line between physical and remote is not fixed: when power controls frequency, power becomes timing.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: What a desync enables, and what defenders see
md: Desync detection is a comparison problem. Log a connection or request identifier at both the front end and the back end, and alert when the request counts or request lines for the same connection differ.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting, responding, and practising safely
md: Desync and cache attacks are the same lesson twice: when two components interpret one message differently, an attacker chooses the difference. Remove ambiguity (HTTP/2 upstream, strict parsing, origin-declared caching), detect disagreement by comparing tiers, and clean up stored state after every fix.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
md: Huge pages are a trade: TLB reach and shorter walks against contiguity, alignment and memory overhead. Use a hugetlbfs pool when you need certainty, THP in madvise mode when the hot regions are known, and check the counters, because both mechanisms fall back silently.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Local, shared and parallel attention, and converting a Transformer
md: Choosing a layout: global attention layers buy exact recall at any distance for a growing KV cache; sliding windows cap the cache and cap exact recall with it; shared attention saves parameters, not cache; parallel heads keep a little attention, and a little KV, in every layer. Across these designs the published choices cluster around a small share of global attention, about 1 layer in 4 to 1 in 8, spread evenly.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT
md: A common mistake is to treat a plant like an office network: run an aggressive vulnerability scan, push patches overnight, reboot to clean an infection. NIST warns that indiscriminate use of IT practices in OT 'may cause availability and timing disruptions'. In OT the security team works with control engineers, not around them.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How attacks on physical processes work
md: Three layers stood between the change and an overflow: humans watching the HMI (defeated by the replay), network monitoring (raised an alert at minute 10), and an independent safety system with its own sensor (tripped at minute 26). Design so that the last layer does not share any path with the first two.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Rules and maps: NERC CIP, IEC 62443, NIST, CISA and ATT&CK for ICS
md: Frameworks tell you what good looks like (62443, NIST), what is mandatory in your sector (NERC CIP for the bulk grid), and how attackers behave (ATT&CK for ICS). Use all three, but remember the cases: most real compromises came through remote access, default passwords and flat networks.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: OIDC as the modern alternative: the same job in JSON
md: SAML and OIDC answer the same questions: who issued this, about whom, for which app, for which login, until when, signed with which key. Learn the questions, and either protocol's fields become a checklist.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: The federation defender's checklist, and where to practise
md: Federation turns identity into a few keys and a trust list. Guard those like domain controllers, verify assertions with libraries that use only what was signed, keep sessions short and revocable, and join IdP and app logs so a login that the IdP never issued stands out.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: PAM vaults: check-out, rotation, and the Uber 2022 script
md: A PAM vault turns many secrets into one, rotates them after use, and ideally never shows them to people. That makes the vault and its administrators the most valuable target you own: protect them as the top of the control plane.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu always returns a threshold, even when nothing changed. On a pair with pure noise it will happily split the noise into two classes and flag a large fraction of the image. Check for a clear gap (or a minimum difference between class means) before trusting the mask.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Declaring, severity, the incident commander and the first hour
md: The IC decides and coordinates; they should not also be the person typing commands. When the IC is debugging, nobody is commanding.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Eradication and recovery: rebuild, credentials, krbtgt and backups
md: Replication is not backup. Synchronised copies (domain controllers, mirrored disks, cloud sync) receive the attacker's deletions and encryption as fast as your legitimate changes. Keep at least one copy offline and immutable, and practise restoring it.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Why escaping is fragile
md: Denylist filters ("block quotes, OR, UNION and --") are escaping's weaker cousin. They reject real input such as O'Brien, and they only stop the spellings someone thought of: SQL accepts comments, different case, different whitespace and many equivalent expressions. Lesson 9 shows a real product whose cleaning function was bypassed by finding a path where it was not applied.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Links, drains, timeouts and a CQ that never overflows
md: Size the **CQ** for the maximum number of completions that can be outstanding (including several per request for multishot operations, which post many completions from one request, lesson 5), not the SQ. Use `IORING_SETUP_CQSIZE` with `cq_entries`, and reap promptly.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Hands on the chip: fault injection, and code that resists it
md: Hardening raises cost; it does not make a chip invulnerable. The RP2350 errata show two glitches defeating an OTP lock-down (E21) and a glitch that changed which data was signature-checked (E24), both on a chip designed with fault attacks in mind. That is why lesson 8 insists that no unit holds a secret whose loss affects other units.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Prototypes: where a missing property comes from
md: Reading a missing property silently falls through to the prototype chain, ending at Object.prototype, which nearly every object shares. The keys `__proto__` and `constructor` (then `prototype`) lead from an ordinary object to that shared object. `Object.create(null)` objects have no chain to follow.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Middleware and internal headers: the Next.js bypass
md: Headers that mean something internally (recursion markers, "already authenticated", forwarded client IPs) must either be stripped at the edge or carry proof that only your own infrastructure can produce. And never let one layer be the only authorisation check: Vercel's own advice is not to use middleware as "the sole method of protecting routes".

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: Cross-thread frees, idle caches and returning memory
md: Published benchmarks (including those in mimalloc's README and report) measure specific workloads. Allocator rankings change with object sizes, thread counts and cross-thread patterns. Measure throughput, p99 latency (the 99th percentile: the time that 99 percent of requests beat) and RSS (resident set size, the memory actually held in RAM) on your own service, with production-like load, before and after switching.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Why the winner changes when the shape changes
md: A common bug is a tuning cache keyed on the kernel name alone, or on batch size only. It never misses, so it never re-tunes, and it silently serves a configuration chosen for a different shape. The symptom is a kernel that is fast in the benchmark that tuned it and mediocre everywhere else.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Worked example: how SPDK reaches 10 million IOPS on one thread
md: Measure with the right tool. SPDK reports up to 2.6 times more IOPS per core using its own `perf` example tool than using fio (the Flexible I/O Tester, the standard Linux storage benchmark) with the SPDK plugin for 4 KiB random reads, because fio's flexibility costs cycles. A slow benchmark harness can hide a fast driver.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels
md: The teacher's knowledge is its input-to-output mapping, including how much probability it gives to each wrong answer. Distillation transfers that mapping by using the teacher's full output distribution as the training target.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Distilling language models: word-level and sequence-level
md: Word-level KD matches the teacher's full next-token distribution at every position of a fixed sequence and needs its probabilities. Seq-KD trains on the teacher's own output text with plain cross-entropy and needs only text. Both train on prefixes the student did not write.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sharing keys and values across heads: MQA and GQA
md: GQA does not reduce attention FLOPs per query head: each query head still scores every cached token. It reduces the bytes stored and read, which is what decode is bound by.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe
md: Smaller caches only become speed if the attention kernel reads the compressed form directly. Dequantizing to BF16 in a separate pass gives back most of the memory traffic saved.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
md: Choose eviction by reuse pattern, not habit. LRU is a fine default; workloads with known future reuse (queued multi-turn sessions, scheduled agent steps) do much better with placement driven by the scheduler.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Why one vector per document leaves accuracy behind
md: Late interaction = independent encoding (so documents are precomputed) + token-level matching at query time (so fine-grained evidence is not averaged away into one vector).

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: The continuous thought: hidden state in, hidden state out
md: Misconception: a continuous thought is not the embedding of the most likely next word. It is never rounded to any vocabulary entry. Decoding it with the LM head is a diagnostic only.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs
md: Loss of auditability is a design cost, not a detail. Latent thoughts can be probed with the LM head, but there is no readable trace to check. Pfau et al. raise the same concern: hidden computation can drift away from anything a human, or a behavior-based safety check, can read.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
md: Bounded search costs the leaf's worst-case error on every lookup. Exponential search costs the error of this lookup. Tight models favour bounded search; loose models with mostly good predictions favour exponential search.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Pointwise, pairwise and listwise approaches
md: A common mix-up: these families describe the **training loss**, not the model. A listwise-trained model still scores each document independently at serving time, so serving cost is the same for all three.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
md: Bigger is not a free fix. Raising $d_k$ raises capacity, but state size and per-token compute grow as $d_k d_v$. The research direction instead is a smarter write rule, which is the next lesson.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Users, groups and root: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
md: Setting a user's shell to `/usr/sbin/nologin` or putting `*` in their password field does not fully disable them. The passwd manual notes such users may still run jobs through cron or log in by other means, and an SSH key in their home directory still works if the shell allows it. To retire an account, lock it, expire it and remove its keys.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: SSH: keys versus passwords, authorized_keys and hardening
md: Keys beat passwords because nothing guessable or reusable travels to the server. That moves the risk to the key files themselves: `authorized_keys` decides who gets in, so audit it like you audit sudoers.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: CIS Benchmarks: what one recommendation contains
md: CIS Benchmarks are consensus-written, product-specific configuration baselines with Level 1, Level 2 and STIG profiles. Each recommendation has a rationale, an audit check and a remediation, and maps to other frameworks, so one automated check can serve several auditors.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Writing audit rules that answer real questions
md: Write rules for questions, give every rule a key, use auid>=1000 together with auid!=unset, write b32 and b64 rules on x86-64, put never rules first, keep syscall rules few, and end production rule sets with -e 2.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Linux EDR and fleet telemetry: what sensors see and miss
md: Every sensor has a layer it watches and layers it cannot. Syscall hooks miss io_uring; host tools miss userland rootkits; nothing on the host reliably reports its own removal. Combine kernel-side sensors at LSM or kprobe level with off-host silence alerts.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a fleet plan, and where to practise
md: Inventory, patch, baseline, sandbox, watch, rebuild. Each is ordinary engineering on its own; run together as a loop on every host, they turn a fleet from 2,000 separate risks into one system you can measure.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: LLM judges for generation: modes, biases and fixes
md: A safe default for generation judging: pairwise or rubric grading with the explanation before the verdict; both orders, with disagreement treated as a tie; report and control length; a judge outside the model families being compared; and a human-labelled subset to measure agreement before every major change.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
md: Continuous batching does **not** mean padding requests to a common length. The tokens are packed with no padding, and only attention looks at per-request boundaries. TensorRT-LLM's in-flight batching explicitly requires packed (unpadded) inputs for this reason.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: How vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM put it together
md: Strip away names and every engine is the same loop: a scheduler spending a per-step token budget, a block allocator answering whether it fits, and a policy for when it does not. The engines differ mainly in that last policy and in how they reuse cached blocks.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Designing the filter schema: enums, ranges and nulls
md: A required, non-nullable field such as `salary_max: integer` forces the model to produce a number even when the user said nothing about salary. Constrained decoding guarantees *some* integer, so you get an invented bound (for example 0, or a number copied from a few-shot example) and a filter that silently removes good results.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Latency: the dependency chain decides, not the call count
md: Parallelism is a latency lever, not a cost lever. Running 100 pointwise calls at once reads the same 22,000 tokens as running them one by one, and on a hosted API it uses up rate limits faster.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pairwise ranking prompting: allpairs, sorting and sliding
md: Pairwise preferences are not guaranteed to be transitive: the model can prefer A over B, B over C and C over A. Allpair just counts wins and copes; sorting algorithms assume a consistent comparator, so their output can depend on which pairs they happened to ask. The PRP paper reports robust results anyway but flags this as an open issue.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
md: Float descriptors (SIFT) are compared with L2 distance; binary descriptors (ORB) with Hamming distance. Binary descriptors trade some distinctiveness for much cheaper extraction, storage and comparison.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
md: Garbage collection does not make ABA go away in general. Michael points out that if a program moves the same node back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a stale CAS can still succeed even with perfect GC. What GC (and the schemes in lesson 6) do prevent is the special case where ABA comes from *freeing and reusing* a node someone still references.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: How accurate is this really, and by which metric
md: Vocabulary trap. "Parsing accuracy" in the 2019 benchmark means grouping, not token-level correctness. Modern papers reserve **PA**, short for parsing accuracy, for the stricter message-level metric where every static token *and* every parameter must be identified correctly, and use **GA** for grouping. A number quoted without its metric is worthless, so always ask: grouping or tokens, per message or per template?

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The pipeline: collect, ship, parse, enrich, store
md: Monitor the pipeline like a production service: events per source per hour, parse-failure rate, queue depth, and the age of the newest event. A sensor that stops sending looks exactly like a quiet, safe network. Also alert on deliberate blinding: Windows event 1102 (Security log cleared) and CloudTrail StopLogging or DeleteTrail calls are ATT&CK Defense Impairment techniques (T1685.005, T1685.002).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Threat hunting and the Pyramid of Pain: the FireEye alert
md: Use indicators (hashes, IPs, domains) for fast, cheap blocking and for searching history after a report is published. Invest your engineering time in behaviour detections, because they are the ones that still work next month.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
md: Online softmax makes attention over KV blocks order-independent. Ring Attention exploits that: queries stay put, KV blocks travel around the ring, and each host needs memory proportional to its block, not to the full sequence.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
md: Convergence is not automatic. The toy update halves the distance to its fixed point each step (it is **contractive**); a learned block carries no such guarantee. Some loops diverge, and Huginn's analysis (lesson 7) finds tokens whose states orbit or drift instead of settling.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
md: Fine-tuning a pretrained model seems to move it along very few useful directions. LoRA turns that observation into an engineering bet: the *change* to each weight matrix during adaptation has low rank (the rank of a matrix is how many independent directions its outputs can point in), so it can be trained and stored as a small factorized update.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
md: Exact unlearning means the result is what retraining without the forget set would give. SISA keeps that guarantee by confining each point's influence to one shard and one suffix of slices, so only that part is retrained.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
md: NIST notes that most samples blend several categories, so the classic labels are 'considerably less useful than they used to be' for incident handling. Use the labels to communicate quickly; spend your time on behaviour and detection.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Behaviours as indicators: persistence, credentials, ransomware
md: Every behaviour rule has false positives: per-user installers for chat and sync clients legitimately write Run keys from AppData. Sigma's falsepositives field is not decoration; tune with an allowlist of known-good signed programs and review what fires.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Truncation does not make the encoder cheaper. Sentence Transformers' docs stress that a Matryoshka model is not faster or smaller to run. What gets cheaper is everything after encoding: storing, indexing and comparing the vectors.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: SP adds no communication volume: a ring all-reduce is literally a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, so TP + SP moves the same bytes as TP. It just stops storing replicated activations. Per layer memory becomes sbh(34 + 5as/h) / t: everything divided by t.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Finding processes: walking the list versus scanning for tags
md: Scanning finds what the list misses, and also things that are no longer true: exited processes and stale copies of live ones. A psscan-only entry with an exit time is history; one without an exit time whose PID is not in the list is the interesting case.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Case: Ivanti Connect Secure, and a memory-first workflow
md: Memory is where code without files, decrypted configs, live connections and the attacker's last commands live, and it is the first evidence to disappear. Capture it early, verify it, and trust only what two independent views agree on.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Why two threads can disagree about what happened first
md: Reordering is invisible to the thread that does it and visible to every other thread. Memory orderings are a portable contract about which reorderings other threads are allowed to observe.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers: announce exactly what you are reading
md: Hazard pointers: publish the address, fence, re-validate, then dereference. Retire into a private list and scan when it reaches R. Garbage is bounded by N x R even if threads stall.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: What memory safety means and why breaking it is dangerous
md: A common misconception: "if it didn't crash, it worked". An out-of-bounds write that lands in another variable usually does not crash at all. The program keeps running with corrupted data, which is often worse than crashing.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Why memory-safe languages remove whole bug classes
md: Memory-safe languages do not make programs bug-free, but they turn the bug classes of this course from silent corruption into compile errors or clean crashes. About two thirds of severe bugs in big C and C++ codebases are memory bugs, so moving new code to memory-safe languages removes most of the worst bugs at the source.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
md: Report mAP alongside rank-1, follow the cross-camera protocol, and compare methods only with the same tricks and the same re-ranking setting, because tricks alone can move rank-1 by about 7 points.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
md: Nearly every Miles feature in this course attacks one of two failure modes: GPUs waiting on each other (throughput), or the trainer computing gradients for something other than what was sampled (fidelity).

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
md: Read the case study's reward numbers the way the report does: the nine-step moving average rose from 0.438 to 0.556 over 100 steps, but one run on one task set cannot separate that from run-to-run variation, so it is an observation, not a measured improvement.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The attacker holds the phone: OWASP MAS and its threat model
md: Misconception: "no root detection" is automatically a finding. MASVS states that the absence of resilience measures "does not in itself constitute a vulnerability". It matters only when the profile includes MAS-R, for example to protect against fraud or cheating.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Local authentication: a fingerprint must unlock a key, not a boolean
md: Misconception: "we use Face ID, so the data is protected by Face ID." Only if the data is encrypted under a key that requires it. If the token sits in UserDefaults or SharedPreferences, the prompt protects nothing from someone with the device's files (lesson 4) or a hook (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Build an MLA layer and prove the two forms agree
md: Checklist when porting MLA: normalize the latent only, and cache the normalized latent; rotate only $q^R$ and $k^R$, with the same pair layout as the checkpoint (interleaved here); scale scores by $1/\sqrt{d_h + d_h^R}$, times the YaRN factor for long-context checkpoints; and compare against the plain form before trusting any speedup.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Batching different adapters: Punica's SGMV kernel
md: SGMV groups rows by adapter and runs all segments in one launch, so a batch can mix adapters while the base matmul stays shared. Its cost grows with the number of distinct adapters and their rank, because each one's weights must be read.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Use multi-query when recall is the bottleneck because users word things differently from the corpus, and the next stage can absorb more candidates. Skip it for precise lookups, compound questions (decompose instead), tight latency budgets, and pipelines where a fixed reranker budget already decides the outcome. Measure end-to-end, not just first-stage recall.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not
md: These are intuitions, not proofs. The paper itself titles this section 'Why does it work? Some speculation'. Treat them as reasons MTP could help, then check the experiments.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
